model-based fMRI can be used to study the neural correlates of human decision making in social contexts.

1) model-based fMRI can be used to identify the neurobiological substrates of complex social decision making in humans and 2) these same models can be used to design objective, model-based measures of social dysfunction in patients with neuropsychiatric disorders.
the human brain has a neural mechanism that is similar to that of the animal models and that this neural mechanism is engaged by social interactions.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of new model-based functional imaging paradigms to probe the neural basis of social interaction in humans.
developing a new generation of computational and experimental approaches to study social behavior and its dysfunction in neuropsychiatric disorders.
developing a quantitative framework for understanding how the brain represents the value of social information and uses it to guide behavior.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the application of computational models to the study of human social behavior is in its infancy, but the potential to provide a mechanistic and quantitative understanding of the neurobiological basis of social decision making is great.
the application of model-driven approaches to the study of human interaction is still in its infancy.

model-based approaches are useful for understanding social decision making, but the field has not yet reached a point of maturity that would allow us to make definitive statements regarding the role of the dopamine system in social behavior.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the application of computational models to the study of social behavior in humans has provided a new window into the neural mechanisms of social reward.
the human brain is capable of making decisions about social interactions, and that these decisions are made by the same reward-prediction machinery that guides other types of decisions.

we are using computational models of social decision making in conjunction with functional neuroimaging techniques to identify neural substrates underlying social behavior in healthy and clinical populations, and to develop novel therapeutic interventions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of computational models in social neuroscience can provide new and unique insight into the neurobiology of social behavior.

model-based functional magnetic resonance imaging can be used to identify neural circuitry underlying social decision making and that these same approaches may be used to assess the impact of social decision making in psychiatric illness.

the application of computational approaches to human interaction can help identify the neural substrates of complex social processes and, in the future, help to identify new biomarkers of psychiatric disease.
